en: Mayon Volcano has erupted many times in the last hundred years, so nearby families often remember more than one eruption.
Mount Pinatubo stayed quiet for a very long time, then in 1991 produced one of the largest eruptions of the last hundred years.
In the Philippines, some volcanoes erupt often while others stay quiet for decades, so the pattern is not the same for every mountain.
Philippine volcanoes sit on the Ring of Fire, where one plate dives under another, so magma keeps rising and eruptions keep happening.
Most Philippine eruptions in the last hundred years have been smaller than Pinatubo in 1991, so giant blasts are rare in the record.
Taal Volcano erupted in 1965 and again in 2020, showing a volcano can rest for decades and then wake quite suddenly.
After an eruption, heavy rain can turn loose ash into lahars for years, a repeating hazard that follows many Philippine blasts.
PHIVOLCS writes down each eruption so scientists and communities can compare today's unrest with patterns from the last hundred years.
Kanlaon on Negros has sent up ash and steam several times in recent decades, a pattern of restless but often smaller events.
Bulusan in Sorsogon also wakes with ash explosions now and then, so nearby towns treat unrest as a repeating risk.
Hibok-Hibok on Camiguin erupted in 1951, a reminder from the last hundred years that a quiet island volcano can still wake.
Scientists watch earthquakes, gas, and ground swelling before many eruptions, but they still cannot name the exact day from the pattern alone.
A volcano that erupts often, like Mayon, is not safer just because people are used to it; each new unrest still needs watching.
Pinatubo's 1991 eruption showed a long-quiet volcano can still hold a very large blast after a long rest.
Records from the last hundred years show Philippine eruptions can send ash, lava, or fast hot flows, not only one kind of event.
Communities near Taal watch steaming and small quakes because those signs have come before several of its modern eruptions.
Eruptions in the Philippines can happen in any month, but rainy months make fresh ash more likely to turn into mudflows.
Mayon often sends lava slowly down its slopes, a pattern that can give nearby towns more time than a sudden explosion would.
Some eruptions start with steam and a little ash, then grow stronger, so early PHIVOLCS reports matter even when the first event looks small.
Talking with elders about past eruptions helps a family see whether their volcano tends to wake often or only after a long rest.
PHIVOLCS lists about two dozen volcanoes as active, which means they have erupted in recent times or still show unrest.
Mayon has erupted about fifty times since 1616, a long record that helps people see how often it tends to wake.
Some years several Philippine volcanoes show unrest close together, while other years stay quieter, so activity comes in uneven clusters.
Ash from an eruption usually falls downwind, so towns on one side of a volcano may be dusty while the other side stays clearer.
PHIVOLCS alert levels rise and fall as unrest changes, a pattern communities use to decide when to prepare or when to go home.
Many Philippine volcanoes are steep stratovolcanoes, so hot flows and rocks often race down the same valleys used in past eruptions.
Taal is a wide caldera with a lake, while Mayon is a tall cone, so their eruption patterns and hazards do not look the same.
A long quiet period does not mean a volcano is finished; the next unrest often begins with quakes and extra gas before any ash.
Hazard maps from past eruptions show which rivers and slopes were hit before, helping families talk about where danger tends to return.
The 1991 Pinatubo eruption sent so much ash and gas high into the air that it briefly cooled climate around the world.
In several recent eruptions, people left early when alerts rose, a pattern that saves lives because the biggest blast may come later.
After Pinatubo, lahars kept flowing in rainy years, showing that the danger pattern can last long after the volcano grows quiet again.
Past eruptions help people see what a volcano can do, but they do not make the next blast perfectly predictable like a clock.
Family stories about past eruptions plus PHIVOLCS records together show whether a nearby volcano tends to wake often or rarely.
Mayon showed strong unrest in 2018 with lava and ash, one more event in its long pattern of waking many times in a century.
Taal's 2020 eruption sent ash across nearby provinces, a sudden event after years of quieter steaming in the lake.
Seismometers, gas sensors, and satellites help PHIVOLCS see repeating signs of unrest that people on the ground might miss at first.
PHIVOLCS keeps a permanent danger zone around some active volcanoes because past eruptions kept hitting the same close slopes.
Many Philippine volcanoes have thick, sticky magma, so they more often blast ash and rocks than pour out very runny lava.
After many eruptions, farms nearby are buried in ash for a time, then later the soil can become rich again, a slow recovery pattern.
The Philippines sits where plates push together, so volcanoes and earthquakes keep happening in the same broad belts over the last century.
PHIVOLCS counts steam-driven explosions as eruptions too, so the pattern includes small events, not only famous giant blasts.
When Mayon is erupting, people sometimes see a night glow on the summit, a repeating sign that hot lava is near the crater.
The same low valleys and river barangays are often asked to leave first, because past eruptions sent flows down those same paths.
Scientists have much clearer eruption records for the last hundred years than for older times, because instruments and agencies now watch daily.
A volcano with no eruption this year can still be active; the last hundred years show long rests between some of the biggest events.
Ash-rich eruption clouds can make lightning, a pattern seen in several modern Philippine eruptions when the plume rises fast and dry.
Comparing Mayon's many eruptions with Pinatubo's rare giant blast helps families see that nearby volcanoes can follow very different clocks.
Before some eruptions the ground slowly swells as magma rises, then sinks after the event, a rise-and-fall pattern instruments can track.
Before some Taal unrest, fish in the lake have died when the water changed, a local sign people have noticed in more than one year.
Airlines reroute around ash clouds after eruptions, because even a modest Philippine blast can send ash high enough to hurt engines.
Towns near active volcanoes practice listening for PHIVOLCS alerts, because the last hundred years show unrest can grow over hours or days.
Bicol has more than one active volcano, so families there may see ash from Mayon at some times and from Bulusan at others.
Fast hot flows tend to follow the same valleys used in earlier eruptions, so old deposit maps still help people guess the next paths.
Taal's 1911 eruption is one of the deadly events still talked about, showing a lake volcano can be dangerous more than once in a century.
People near some volcanoes notice a stronger rotten-egg gas smell when unrest grows, a repeating clue that magma or hot rock is closer.
The Philippines has many earthquakes that never lead to an eruption, so a single shake is not by itself a volcano pattern.
When an alert level later drops, families may go home, but they keep watching because some volcanoes grow restless again within the same decade.
Schools near Mayon or Taal often cancel class when alerts rise, a community pattern learned from eruptions in the last hundred years.
Discussing past eruptions with family and neighbors helps a class see that patterns exist, even though no volcano follows a perfect timetable.
In a fair test, scientists repeat the same measurement at least three times so one lucky or unlucky result cannot decide the answer.
source: DepEd MATATAG G6; encyclopedia-stable scientific method

en: A fair test changes only one thing at a time so you can tell which change caused the new result.
Everything you are not testing must stay the same, including tools, amounts, and waiting time, or the comparison is no longer fair.
Scientists write down each trial as they go, because a result you only remember later is easy to mix up or round wrongly.
Use the same ruler, balance, or timer for every trial so a change in the number is not just a change of instrument.
After three or more trials, many investigations use the average so one odd measurement does not pull the answer too far.
If you compare two mixtures, start with the same amount of water and the same size of container, or the test is unfair.
When you time a change of state, wait the same number of minutes in every trial so extra time is not mistaken for a better method.
Replication means doing the whole test again the same way, not just looking once and deciding the first look was enough.
If you change both the amount and the temperature at once, you cannot tell which change made the mixture behave differently.
Look at samples at the same stage of the test, such as after five minutes, so you are comparing like with like.
Accurate measuring means using the marks on the tool carefully and not guessing the last digit from far away.
Place a balance on a level table before you weigh, because a tilted scale can make every trial read a little high or low.
Do the trials in the same room temperature and light when you can, so weather in the classroom is not a hidden extra change.
Label every cup or bag before you mix anything, so a fair test is not ruined by mixing up which sample is which.
If one trial looks very different, do not hide it; repeat the measurement to see whether it was a mistake or a real result.
Before you start, name the one thing you will change, such as the kind of salt, so the rest of the plan can stay fair.
Name the thing you will measure as your result, such as how many minutes until the solid disappears, and stick to that measure.
Write a short list of what you will keep the same, like water volume and stirring, so helpers do not quietly change the fair test.
If one mixture is stirred fast and another is only swirled once, you have changed two things, and the test is no longer fair.
Set a digital balance to zero with the empty cup on it before each trial so the cup's weight is not counted as extra mass.
When you measure water in a cylinder, read the bottom of the curve at eye level so every trial uses the same reading habit.
Stopping a trial early because you already like the result makes the test unfair; finish the planned time for every run.
A fair investigation shares the raw numbers from all trials, not only the one trial that looks neatest on a poster.
If several classmates measure, they should agree first on how to read the scale, so person-to-person habits are not a hidden variable.
Repeating the whole fair test on another day is a strong check, because it shows the result was not just one classroom afternoon.
Keep one sample unchanged as a comparison, so you can see what happens when you do nothing as well as when you change one thing.
Count drops, crystals, or bubbles with a plan, instead of saying 'many' or 'few', so later trials can be compared with numbers.
Use the same brand and lot of baking soda or salt across trials, because a different packet can hide a second unwanted change.
Start and stop every trial with the same clock or timer, and say the start out loud so partners record the same seconds.
Wash and dry glassware between trials, because leftover powder from the last run can change the next result without you meaning to.
Write the steps and the data table before you mix anything, so you are not inventing a new method halfway through the trials.
Write the unit beside every number, such as grams or milliliters, so a later reader does not compare unlike measurements by mistake.
Three trials means the same test three times, not three different ideas tried once each, which would not be a fair comparison.
A partner can watch the scale while you pour, then both of you record the number, which reduces simple reading mistakes.
Choosing only the trial you like best is not honest science; a fair report keeps all good measurements in the set.
If you drop an object to test a change, drop it from the same height every time, or height becomes a second hidden variable.
Check that a timer still matches a known clock, and that a ruler starts at zero, before you trust a long set of trials.
When counting bubbles or drips, agree on a quiet count so two people are not adding extra events that only one of them heard.
Cut or weigh samples so they start the same size, because a bigger piece can change faster and trick you about the method.
If the power flickers or someone bumps the table, write that in the notes beside the trial instead of pretending the number is clean.
Start with a question you can test fairly, such as which solid dissolves faster in the same warm water, not a question you cannot measure.
A surprising result is a reason to repeat the trial, not a reason to stop and tell a story that has only one measurement behind it.
Ask watchers not to stir, heat, or add water 'to help', because extra help is an unplanned change that spoils a fair test.
Say 'start' only when everything is ready, so one trial does not secretly include extra mixing time that the others did not get.
A simple graph is more trustworthy after you have at least three careful trials, because two points can make a line that is only luck.
Keep the extra digits while you work, and round only at the end, so early rounding does not hide small but real differences.
If the test uses heat, use the same stove setting or the same sunny windowsill, or the heat itself becomes an extra variable.
Pick a cylinder or balance that can hold the whole amount, because a tool that overflows cannot give a fair number for that trial.
If you already hope one mixture wins, label cups with letters so hope does not make you stop the clock a little early.
A photo of the setup helps you put everything back the same way for trial two and trial three after you wash the cups.
Use water from the same bottle or tap for every trial, because water from two places may differ in minerals and temperature.
Agree what 'finished' looks like, such as no solid left on the bottom, so every trial is stopped by the same rule, not by feeling.
If the first three trials disagree a lot, do more trials instead of picking a winner, because disagreement is a signal to measure again.
Write one sentence that says exactly how you did the test, so another group could repeat it and check your pattern.
Wear the same safe gear in every trial, and never skip a safety step to go faster, because a fair test is still a safe test.
A fair test is a careful comparison: change one thing, keep the rest the same, measure accurately, and repeat at least three times.
A simple investigation starts by writing a clear problem, such as which material dries faster, so you know what you are trying to find out.
Turn the problem into a question you can test, not a story, so the next steps have a real job to do.
List every material before you begin, including cups, water, and a timer, so you are not hunting for tools in the middle of a step.
Write only the materials the test needs, because extra bottles and powders on the table make it easy to use the wrong one.
Write the steps in order before you mix or heat anything, so each person in the group does the same investigation.
Do one written step at a time and check it off, because skipping ahead is how groups lose the comparison they planned.
After you finish the steps, write what you found out in plain words, using your measurements, not only what you hoped would happen.
A good finding answers the problem you wrote at the start, even if the answer is 'they were about the same'.
Pick a problem you can test with school materials in one lesson, not a question that needs a giant laboratory.
A simple drawing of the setup is part of planning what you need to do, and it helps the group put the tools in the right places.
Include safety gear in the materials list, such as goggles if you might splash, so safety is a step and not an afterthought.
Decide who will pour, who will time, and who will write, so the steps happen together instead of everyone grabbing the same cup.
You may guess what will happen, but the investigation still has to test the guess with materials and steps, not with arguing.
Gather every listed material on a tray first, then start the steps, so a missing spoon does not pause the test halfway.
Record numbers while you do the steps, not after you pack up, because memory mixes trials once the table is clean.
When you write what you learned, point to the evidence, such as 'cup A lost more water', not only 'I think A is better'.
If the first problem is too big, shrink it, such as testing two fabrics instead of ten, so the steps still fit the lesson.
Put amounts on the materials list, such as 100 milliliters of water, so 'some water' does not mean a different amount each time.
Good steps say how long to wait, how many times to stir, and what to look for, so the doing part is not a guess.
What you found out can surprise you; an honest investigation reports the surprise instead of changing the numbers to match the first guess.
A clear problem names what you will compare, such as wet soil versus dry soil, so the materials and steps have a purpose.
Tick each item on the materials list as you set it out, the way cooks check a recipe, so the doing steps are not missing a tool.
Keep the written steps in the notebook while you work, because a plan that lives only in someone's head is easy to change by accident.
The finding is what the test showed, not a grade for the group; a careful test can still show that your first idea was wrong.
If you cannot say what you would measure, the problem is not ready yet, and you should sharpen it before listing materials.
Put a notebook or data table in the materials, because 'what you need to do' includes a place to catch the numbers.
Practice the timing step once with empty cups if the group is new, then do the real investigation with the listed materials.
Say the finding out loud in one or two sentences so the group agrees on what was learned before packing the materials away.
Write the problem in words a classmate can read once, because a tangled sentence makes the later steps harder to follow.
Choose materials the classroom already has, such as spoons, cups, and tap water, so the investigation can actually be carried out.
The last doing step is cleanup: pour leftovers where the teacher says, wash tools, and dry the table so the next group can start.
Sometimes what you found out is 'we need another test', and that is a real result when the first steps could not decide.
Ask 'which dries faster' or 'what happens if', not a huge why that no classroom test can answer in one afternoon.
If the problem is about melting, the materials should include something that can melt safely, plus a way to tell when it has melted.
Number the steps 1, 2, 3 so the group can point to the same line when someone asks 'what do we need to do now'.
Write what you learned as a complete sentence that a parent could understand, not as a single word such as 'yes' or 'hot'.
Show the teacher the problem and the materials list before mixing, so an unsafe or untestable plan can be fixed early.
A photo of the materials and of the result can help you remember what you did when you write what you found out later.
If you suddenly want a new idea, finish the written plan first; extra ideas belong in a new investigation with a new problem.
A strong 'what we learned' sentence names both the answer and the clue, such as 'the dark cloth dried first, in twenty minutes'.
In a matter lesson the problem should be about materials, such as mixing, melting, or drying, so the investigation serves the topic.
If a cup might spill, put a spare cup on the materials list so one accident does not stop the whole investigation.
Read the full 'what we need to do' list aloud once before starting, so quiet group members hear the plan too.
Sometimes the finding is easiest as a tiny table of results plus one sentence, so classmates can see the numbers and the meaning.
Leave the problem written at the top of the page while you work, so the doing steps do not wander into a different question.
If you will measure, the materials list should include the measuring tool, not only the water or the powder you will pour.
Stop when the written steps end and then write the finding; adding extra unplanned tests can scramble what you can honestly claim.
A useful finding can also name a next question, such as 'would the same cloth dry slower in a closed room'.
A simple science plan can fit on one page: the problem, the materials, the steps to do, and what you found out.

topic: do not copy a friend's finding
en: Write what your own steps showed, even if a nearby group found something else; copying a finding skips the investigation.
Put fair-test words in the problem when you can, such as 'same amount of water', so the later steps stay honest.
Set materials where every group member can reach them safely, so the doing steps do not become a fight over one spoon.
Looking closely is part of what you need to do: watch color, bubbles, or wetness, then write those clues beside the time.
When you can say the problem, the materials, the steps, and the finding, the simple investigation has gone all the way around.
When a sounding object moves toward you, its sound waves bunch up, so you hear a higher pitch than when it stands still.
When a sounding object moves away from you, its sound waves stretch out, so you hear a lower pitch than before.
If you walk quickly toward a ringing bell, you meet more waves each second, so the bell sounds a little higher.
If you walk away from a ringing bell, you meet fewer waves each second, so the same bell sounds a little lower.
The faster a horn moves toward you, the more the waves bunch, so the rise in pitch is greater than for a slow horn.
A moving horn can also get louder as it comes near, but the Doppler change is about pitch, which is how high or low it sounds.
In front of a moving sound source the wavelength is shorter, so the frequency is higher for a listener standing there.
Behind a moving sound source the wavelength is longer, so a listener there hears a lower frequency.
If both the sound source and the listener stay still, the pitch does not slide up or down from motion.
A jeepney horn can sound higher as it comes along the road and lower after it passes, even though the driver did not change the horn.
A train horn often drops in pitch right after the train goes by, a everyday clue that the source has started moving away.
The speed of sound in still air stays about the same; motion of the source changes wavelength and frequency, not that air speed.
Pitch goes up when more sound waves reach your ear each second, which is what a moving-closer source does to the wave train.
Sound can change if the source moves, if you move, or if both move, because what matters is how you close the gap.
If you ride beside a sounding truck at about the same speed, the pitch shift is small because you are not closing or opening the gap fast.
A classmate walking toward you while humming can sound slightly higher than the same hum when that classmate walks away.
A buzzing toy swung in a circle sounds higher when it comes toward your ear and lower when it swings away.
A motorcycle engine often seems to drop in note as it races past, even if the rider did not ease off the throttle at that instant.
The pitch change from motion is not the same as an echo; an echo is a bounce, while Doppler is a change in how waves are spaced.
Wind can carry sound toward you or away, but that is moving the air; Doppler from a horn is the source itself moving through the air.
In this lesson the receiver is whoever hears the sound, such as you on the sidewalk, not only a microphone on a stand.
The source is the thing making the sound, such as a horn, a bell, or a loudspeaker on a moving truck.
The big drop in pitch is often noticed right as the moving source passes you, when it switches from coming closer to going away.
A person standing still beside a road can still hear the Doppler change, because the sounding vehicle is the moving source.
People riding with the horn usually do not hear that sliding pitch, because they are moving with the source instead of past it.
Higher pitch means more wave crests arrive each second; a source racing toward you packs those crests closer together.
Lower pitch means fewer wave crests arrive each second; a source racing away leaves those crests more spread out.
A campaign loudspeaker on a passing tricycle can change note as it goes by, even if the recorded song itself does not change key.
Running toward a loud festival speaker raises the pitch a little for you, because you, the receiver, are moving into the waves.
Running away from the same speaker lowers the pitch a little, because you are moving out of the waves instead of into them.
Two listeners can hear different pitches from one moving horn: the person ahead hears higher, and the person behind hears lower.
If a sound stays at the same distance while it moves, the pitch slide is smaller than when the source races straight at you.
Moving does not remove the need for air: the sound still travels through a medium, while Doppler only changes the spacing of those waves.
The engine or horn may keep making the same sound; what changes for you is how those waves are packed when the source is moving.
A mosquito's buzz can seem to change as it flies past your ear, because the tiny sound source is moving relative to you.
A ferry horn can sound higher as the boat comes into port and lower as it leaves, a waterfront example of a moving sound source.
A smooth slide in pitch as something passes is a clue the source or the listener is moving, not that the object suddenly changed its engine.
Scientists talk about closing speed: how fast the gap between source and listener is shrinking or growing, which sets the size of the shift.
If a horned vehicle races toward you while you run toward it, the pitch rise is larger than if only one of you is moving.
If the source races away while you also run away, even fewer waves reach you each second, so the pitch can fall more.
A teacher can walk past the class with a buzzing phone to show the note rise and fall without needing a real road.

topic: does not change music key inside
en: A song playing inside a moving bus keeps its key for riders; the outside Doppler change is for people the bus is passing.
A very fast source bunches waves more tightly in front, so the approaching pitch can sound much higher than a slow bicycle bell.
Even when the source is moving, sound in air is still a longitudinal wave; Doppler changes the spacing, not the side-to-side idea.
You can test the idea with your ears: stand still, listen to a passing horn, and notice the note drop after it goes by.
A microphone on a moving phone is a receiver too; if it races toward a speaker, the recorded pitch can come out a little high.

topic: not the same as volume fade
en: A far horn is quieter, but quiet is not the same as low pitch; Doppler is the high-to-low change from motion, not only from distance.
A jet high above can change note as it crosses the sky, another moving source, though the boom of a shock wave is a different event.
Draw circles packed on one side of a moving dot to show why a listener on that side hears a higher sound.
On the other side of the same drawing, the circles are more spread out, which is why that listener hears a lower sound.
As long as the source is slower than sound, waves still get ahead of it; they are just closer together in the forward direction.
Once you know the pattern, you can hear it in passing buses, trucks, and tricycles, not only in a science video.
Riding a bike toward a playground bell makes you the moving receiver, so the bell can sound slightly higher than to a sitting friend.
A sitting friend hears less pitch shift from the same bell, because that friend's ears are not moving into the waves.
Naming the Doppler effect is not enough: you explain it by saying the waves bunch when the gap closes and stretch when the gap opens.
One moving loudspeaker can send a slightly higher song to people it approaches and a slightly lower song to people it has passed.
The horn does not secretly retune itself as it drives; your ears hear a different frequency because the wave spacing in the air changed.
You can record a passing horn on a phone, then compare the note before and after it passes to hear the drop more clearly.
Rain getting louder is not the Doppler pitch slide; Doppler is a high-to-low change tied to motion of the source or the listener.
Whenever the gap between a sound and your ear is closing quickly, more waves arrive each second and the pitch tends to rise.
Whenever the gap between a sound and your ear is opening quickly, fewer waves arrive each second and the pitch tends to fall.
Pushing and pulling a slinky along its length is a classroom example of a longitudinal wave, because the coils move back and forth the same way the pulse travels.
Shaking a slinky sideways makes a transverse wave, because the coils move across the direction the pulse travels down the spring.
A wiggle sent along a jump rope is a transverse wave: the rope moves up and down while the wiggle travels toward the other end.
A plucked guitar string is a transverse wave example, because bits of the string move across the string while the wave runs along it.
A radio wave is a transverse electromagnetic wave that can carry a station's signal through space without needing air as a medium.
Microwaves in an oven are transverse electromagnetic waves; they are a different example from the mechanical waves on water or a rope.
Ultrasound used in a clinic is a longitudinal sound wave, because the pulses are compressions traveling through tissue, not a side-to-side rope wiggle.
A tuning fork sending a tone through classroom air is a longitudinal wave example: air particles squeeze and spread along the travel direction.
Thunder is a longitudinal sound wave traveling through air from lightning, so it is an example of a compression wave, not a rope-like wiggle.
Whale song traveling through ocean water is a longitudinal wave example, because sound in water is still a back-and-forth compression wave.
A knock traveling through a wooden desk is a longitudinal wave in a solid: the wood particles push on their neighbors along the path.
Ripples on a pond surface are a common transverse-like water wave: the surface moves mainly up and down as the rings spread outward.
A stadium crowd wave is a transverse-style example: people stand and sit while the 'wave' travels sideways around the stands.
Visible light is a transverse electromagnetic wave, which is why it is grouped with radio and microwaves, not with sound.
X-rays are another transverse electromagnetic example; they travel as changing electric and magnetic fields, not as air compressions.
The infrared beam from a TV remote is a transverse electromagnetic wave, even though you cannot see it with your eyes.
A sonar ping used to find the seafloor is a longitudinal sound wave sent through water, then heard as an echo coming back.
A speaker cone pushing air in and out launches a longitudinal sound wave, a household example of compressions leaving the speaker.

topic: flag in wind not a wave type
en: A flag flapping is moving cloth, not a clean textbook wave; better transverse examples are a shaken rope or a light beam.
Ultraviolet light in sunlight is a transverse electromagnetic wave, which is why it is listed with light, not with thunder.
A mobile phone call travels as transverse radio waves through the air and space around you, then becomes sound only in the speaker.
A clap in a gym is a longitudinal sound example; the bang you hear is air being compressed, then spreading, along the path to your ear.
Gently shaking a basin of water makes surface waves you can class with transverse examples, because the surface mostly moves up and down.
A pulse sent down a long spring lying on the floor, by pushing the end, is a longitudinal example you can see as a bunching of coils.
A Wi-Fi signal is a transverse electromagnetic wave example, even though we notice it only when a phone or laptop receives it.
A bowed violin string is a transverse wave on the string; the sound that later reaches your ear is a different, longitudinal wave in air.
A P-wave from an earthquake is a longitudinal example in rock, while people also list sound as a longitudinal example in air.
An S-wave from an earthquake is a transverse example in rock, grouped with rope waves rather than with sound.
Light from a classroom lamp is a transverse wave example that does not need a slinky, a rope, or air to travel across the room.
A shout down a hallway is a longitudinal sound example; naming it helps you remember everyday compressional waves, not only lab springs.
Long ocean swells arriving at a beach are water-surface waves often classed with transverse examples, even though water also moves in circles.
Gamma rays are transverse electromagnetic waves, a high-energy example in the same family as light and radio, not a sound.
A drumhead mostly moves up and down, like a transverse motion, but the boom you hear is a longitudinal wave that then travels in air.
Pulses of light in a fiber-optic cable are transverse electromagnetic waves used to send information, not longitudinal sound pulses.
A helpful notebook page lists longitudinal examples on one side, such as sound and slinky push-pull, and transverse examples on the other.
A phone's buzzing case is a mechanical vibration; the alert you hear across the room is a longitudinal sound wave in air.
Two children holding a rope and sending a bump toward each other are making a transverse wave you can watch in the schoolyard.
Longitudinal waves are also called compressional waves, so sound, ultrasound, and P-waves all belong on that same example list.
Transverse waves in solids are sometimes called shear waves, which is why S-waves sit on the transverse example list with rope waves.

topic: not every wiggle is one type
en: Some real waves mix motions, so scientists pick clear examples: sound for longitudinal, and a shaken rope or light for transverse.
A church bell heard across a plaza is a longitudinal sound example traveling through air from the bell to your ears.
Sunlight reaching Earth is a transverse electromagnetic wave example that traveled through space, where there is almost no air.
Ripple-tank waves on shallow water are a lab example used to show wave shapes, and they are grouped with transverse surface waves.
A tap on a metal rail can send a longitudinal wave along the rail, which is why you may hear the tap through the metal before the air.
You do not need a fancy laser to name a transverse example: a flashlight beam is already a transverse electromagnetic wave.
A kulintang gong heard across a hall is a longitudinal sound-wave example in air, even though the gong itself is a vibrating plate.
A TV broadcast arriving at an antenna is a transverse radio-wave example, later turned into pictures and sounds inside the set.
A quick check: if the example is a sound you hear, it is longitudinal; if it is light or a side-shaken rope, it is transverse.
One earthquake can send both types: a longitudinal P-wave example and a transverse S-wave example traveling through the same ground.
Sound leaving headphones is a longitudinal wave in air, even if the music was stored as numbers and carried earlier by radio waves.

topic: water wave vs sound in water
en: Do not mix the two water examples: surface ripples are classed with transverse waves, while a splash sound in water is longitudinal.
Shaking a long bamboo pole up and down can send a transverse pulse along the pole, a yard example besides a jump rope.
A solid answer names three longitudinal examples, such as sound, slinky push-pull, and P-waves, plus three transverse examples such as rope, light, and S-waves.
The main difference is particle motion: longitudinal particles move along the travel direction, while transverse particles move across it.
A similarity is that both longitudinal and transverse waves carry energy from one place to another without the particles making the whole trip.
Transverse waves show crests and troughs, while longitudinal waves show compressions and rarefactions, two different pictures of the same idea of a cycle.
Both kinds have a wavelength: crest-to-crest for a transverse wave, or compression-to-compression for a longitudinal wave.
Both kinds have frequency, meaning how many cycles pass a point each second, whether the cycle is a wiggle or a squeeze.
Both kinds have amplitude: how far particles move from rest, as height on a rope or as how tightly air is squeezed in a sound.
A difference: sound, a longitudinal mechanical wave, needs a medium, while light, a transverse electromagnetic wave, can travel through empty space.
A similarity is that both kinds can bounce: sound can echo from a wall, and a rope wave can reflect from a held end.
Solids can carry both types, which is why earthquake P-waves and S-waves can both travel through rock, unlike air which does not carry S-waves.
A difference: fluids such as air and water readily carry longitudinal sound, but they do not carry a simple side-to-side S-wave the way rock can.
A similarity is that speed, frequency, and wavelength are still linked for both kinds: faster cycles at the same speed mean a shorter wavelength.
Drawings look different: a transverse wave is a side wiggle, while a longitudinal wave is drawn as crowded and spread-out patches along a line.
Both kinds can bend around openings: sound can go around a doorway, and water waves can spread after passing a gap in a barrier.
Transverse waves can be polarized, which is why polarizing sunglasses cut glare, while a longitudinal sound wave does not polarize that way.
A similarity: in both kinds the wave can move far while each bit of the medium only jiggles in a small region and then returns.
Both kinds need a source of disturbance, such as a vibrating object for sound or a shaken hand for a rope wave.
A similarity is that mechanical waves of either kind change speed when they enter a different medium, such as air versus water versus rock.

topic: sound cannot be transverse in air
en: A difference: you cannot send a lasting side-to-side sound wave through air the way you send a transverse wiggle along a rope.
Both kinds can meet and add or cancel: two sounds can make beats, and two water ripples can make a pattern of still and moving spots.
You can map one cycle to the other: a crest is like a compression, and a trough is like a rarefaction, even though the motions differ.
A similarity is that people use both kinds to send information: sound for talking, and transverse radio or light waves for broadcasts.
A bell jar demo shows a difference: sound dies in a vacuum, but light, a transverse electromagnetic wave, still crosses the empty space.
Both kinds have a period, the time for one full cycle, whether that cycle is a rope bump or one squeeze-and-spread of air.
In both kinds energy travels along the wave, but only transverse waves have a shake that is perpendicular to that energy path.
A similarity is that scientists still use amplitude, wavelength, and frequency symbols for both, even when the pictures on the page look unlike.
P-waves and S-waves from one earthquake make a natural contrast: same event, same rock, two particle motions, two speeds.

topic: both can be drawn as graphs
en: Both can be graphed against time at one place, so a microphone trace of sound and a float bouncing on a ripple can look like similar wiggles.
A difference: a graph of pressure versus time can look like a transverse drawing even when the real wave is longitudinal, so the picture needs a label.
In a rope wave and in a sound wave, energy moves forward while the rope bits and the air bits stay in their neighborhood.
A similarity: rope waves and sound waves are both mechanical when they need a material medium, unlike light which does not.

topic: cannot hear a transverse EM wave
en: A difference: your ear detects longitudinal sound, not the transverse electromagnetic waves of radio or light, which need other sensors.
Both kinds can be a one-time pulse or a repeating train of cycles, so 'wave' does not always mean a long ongoing tone or wiggle.
Amplitude means a bigger disturbance in both, but the picture is height on a transverse rope and extra squeeze in a longitudinal sound.
Sound is slower in air than in water, and rope waves are slower on a heavier rope; in both kinds the medium sets the speed.
To compare them fairly, draw a slinky push-pull beside a slinky side-shake so the only change in the picture is particle direction.
When two waves of either kind overlap, they add their disturbances for a moment, then can pass through and keep going.
A difference: a transverse mechanical wave needs the medium to be able to shear or move sideways, which a thin gas cannot do well.
A longitudinal wave needs the medium to be able to squeeze and spring back along the travel line, which air, water, and solids all can.
A similarity: Earth scientists use both types of earthquake waves to learn what is inside the planet, because they travel differently.

topic: S waves not through liquid outer core
en: A famous difference: S-waves do not travel through Earth's liquid outer core, while P-waves do, which helped map that liquid layer.
Both carry energy, but we feel sound with ears or a drum skin and we detect light with eyes or a solar cell, different sensors for different types.
A similarity is that both can be absorbed: curtains soak up sound, and a dark cloth soaks up light, turning wave energy into a little heat.
A compare-and-contrast table should have at least one similarity, such as energy transfer, and one difference, such as particle direction.
They are two families, not enemies: a single event like an earthquake or a storm can produce more than one kind of wave at once.
A practical difference is how you measure wavelength in a photo: peak to peak on water, or crowded-band to crowded-band on a slinky.
Both kinds can form standing patterns in a bounded space, such as a guitar string for transverse motion and an organ pipe for sound.
A scale difference: light, a transverse electromagnetic wave, is far faster than sound, a longitudinal mechanical wave in air.
A similarity is that the energy they carry came from the source; waves do not create energy from nothing as they travel.
The same slinky can show both types if you change only the shake: push-pull for longitudinal, side-to-side for transverse.
A longitudinal rarefaction is a spread-out region of the medium, not a missing crest; mixing those labels is a common mix-up of the two types.
A similarity is that particles oscillate about a rest place in both kinds; the difference is only the line along which they oscillate.
Even two transverse examples differ: a rope needs a medium, while light does not, so 'transverse' is not the same fact as 'needs air'.
Longitudinal sound can travel in solids, liquids, and gases, a range of media that a simple transverse rope wave does not match.
A similarity: both tend to spread and weaken with distance from the source, which is why a far shout and a far lamp both seem weaker.
A class can act the difference: stand in a line and step forward-back for longitudinal, or sway left-right for transverse, while the 'wave' travels down the line.
In both class acts the children stay in their places after the pulse passes, a similarity that shows energy moved but the people did not travel.
Neither kind is 'better'; each fits different jobs, which is why the competency asks for differences and similarities, not a winner.
A similarity is that each wave has a travel direction you can point to, even when particles in a transverse wave are moving across that arrow.
A difference to keep straight: compressions are crowded particles along the path, not taller bumps; taller bumps belong to transverse crests.
In one sentence: both transfer energy in cycles, but longitudinal cycles squeeze along the path and transverse cycles wiggle across it.
In a ripple tank, the bright moving lines are crests, the high parts of the water wave, which you can watch as they travel across the tray.
The darker bands between those bright lines are troughs, the low parts of the wave, so a full wave is one crest plus one trough.
Wavelength in the tank is the distance from one crest to the next, which you can measure with a ruler on the white screen or tray.
Amplitude is how high a crest rises above the still-water level; a bigger dipper splash makes taller waves in the same tank.
When a straight wave hits a barrier in the tank, it bounces and travels back, a reflection you can see as a second set of lines.
A wave that hits a wall at a slant bounces off at a matching slant, a pattern you can mark with two arrows on the tank diagram.
If you leave a small gap in a barrier, the waves that pass through spread into the quiet water beyond, a bending called diffraction.
When part of a wave front enters shallower water, that part slows and the front can bend, a change of direction you can see in the tank.
A dripping tap or a point dipper makes circular ripples, so you can compare ring-shaped waves with the straight waves from a vibrating bar.
A flashing strobe can freeze the pattern so you can measure crest spacing while the real water is still moving.
Ripple tanks use a thin layer of water so the waves stay easy to light from below and so their shape shows clearly on the screen.
A faster vibrating dipper makes more crests each second, so the pattern looks tighter even if the tank size stays the same.
Start the dipper gently; huge splashes hide crests and troughs, and they are not the careful waves this investigation is meant to show.
Before you start waves, mark the still-water level on a side ruler so later you can tell height of crests from that calm line.
A straight metal barrier in the tank is the wall you use to watch reflection; curve it and the bounced pattern changes shape too.
Two point dippers side by side can make a crisscross pattern where some spots stay almost still, a meeting of waves you can map.
The 'width' of a wave in the tank is the spacing of the moving bands, which is the wavelength you were asked to observe.
The 'height' of a wave in the tank is how much the surface rises and falls, which is the amplitude of those ripples.
Watch which way the bright crest lines move; that direction is the pattern of movement of the wave energy across the tank.
A shallow 'beach' of foam or slope at the far end soaks up waves so they do not bounce back and mess up the pattern you are measuring.
A good investigation record is a drawing of crest lines, arrows for travel, and notes of what happened at walls and gaps.
Level the tray before you add water, because a tilted tank makes one side shallow and secretly bends every wave you try to study.
Keep the water depth the same when you compare two patterns, or you have changed a hidden variable as well as the barrier shape.
Far from a point dipper the rings look almost straight in a small window, so you must look at the whole tank to name the true shape.
Count how many crests pass a mark in ten seconds to compare frequency, a movement feature besides shape and size.
Reflected crests can meet incoming crests and make a busy crisscross near a wall, so look carefully before you name a single travel direction.
A wider gap lets waves go through with less spreading than a tiny gap, a change of pattern you can test with two barrier openings.

topic: do not confuse splash with wave
en: The first messy splash is not the wave feature to describe; wait for the clean moving bands, then talk about crest, trough, and path.
One partner can time or run the dipper while the other draws the pattern, so the group observes instead of chasing spilled water.
The tank is for seeing three features: shape as crests and troughs, size as width and height, and movement as travel, bending, and bounce.
To investigate local sky knowledge, ask an elder for permission first, then listen to how their community named stars or warned about eclipses.
source: DepEd MATATAG G6; oral history method

en: Write or record the exact words you are allowed to keep, so a later reader can tell a community story from your own summary.
Reliable secondary sources, such as museum notes or reviewed books, can sit beside interviews when you cannot travel to a community.

topic: do not treat one voice as all
en: One interview is not the whole Philippines; different islands named different star patterns, so gather more than one local account.

topic: compare story with a star chart
en: After you hear a star-pattern name, compare it with a printed star chart so you can see which lights in tonight's sky the story is about.
Many indigenous sky watchers treated solar and lunar eclipses as events that return, so they watched the Moon's phases to guess when one might come.

topic: lunar eclipse easier to predict locally
en: A lunar eclipse happens at full moon, a pattern people could notice without a telescope, which is why full-moon nights were watched closely.

topic: solar eclipse rarer in one place
en: A solar eclipse is rarer for one village, so stories often mark it as a special darkening of the Sun, not as an everyday calendar tick.
Rising and setting of familiar star groups was used to track hours of the night, a clock that needs no battery, only a clear sky.
Which star pattern shows up after sunset changes with the months, so the night sky also worked as a seasonal calendar for planting and fishing.
When you copy a sky story from a book, write the author and title, so classmates can tell a secondary source from a neighbor's interview.

topic: ask what the pattern was for
en: Ask whether a star group was used to find direction, to time planting, or to tell a story, because one pattern can serve more than one job.
People who tracked time by the Moon counted about twenty-nine to thirty nights from one new moon to the next, a cycle you can still check.
Local names for star groups are data, not jokes; write them carefully, because they are how a community communicated the same lights you see.
A secondary source is an account already written or recorded by someone else, such as an ethnography, not the sky itself and not your guess.
Modern astronomy explains eclipses as the Earth, Moon, and Sun lining up; indigenous watchers still could notice the repeating darkening without that diagram.
For a class investigation, prefer a library book, a museum card, or a named interview over an unsourced post that cannot be checked.

topic: draw the pattern you were told
en: Sketch the star group as the speaker described it, then look up on a clear night to see whether those lights still make that shape.
Some communities tracked time by saying a star group was 'just rising' or 'straight up', everyday words that still point to a clock in the sky.
Saying eclipses follow a pattern is not the same as naming the exact clock time; investigate how people talked about 'soon' versus a numbered date.

topic: sea and farm both used sky
en: Ask separately about farming and about seafaring, because the same night sky can time planting inland and steer a boat along a coast.
If a story is sacred or private, do not paste it on a poster; ask what may be shared with the class, and respect a no.
Collect the local names for new moon, half moon, and full moon, because those words are how people communicated a time cycle you can still observe.
A strong report pairs a community account of an eclipse with a simple scientific diagram, then says what each account is useful for.
Indigenous night watchers could see star groups drift westward overnight, a repeating motion they used as a clock long before wristwatches.

topic: not every bright light is a star
en: When you gather sky stories, ask whether a bright light was a star, a planet, or the Moon, so the pattern you map is the right object.
Write the year of the book or interview, because sky lore can be recorded long after it was used, and that date is part of the evidence.
Some communities used eclipse stories as a warning to stay calm and watch, which is one way they communicated that the darkening would pass.
Sort your notes into three piles: eclipses, night-sky patterns, and timekeeping, matching the three questions this competency asks you to investigate.

topic: look up on a moonless night
en: Star patterns are easier to check on a moonless night, so plan the outdoor test of a story for when the Moon is not washing out the sky.
A source is more reliable when another person could find it again, such as a named book, a museum label, or a recorded interview with a date.
Star names and eclipse sayings were ways of teaching, so your investigation is about how knowledge was communicated, not only about listing pretty pictures.

topic: finish with what you still cannot tell
en: End the report by saying what one interview or one book could not tell you, because honest gathering includes the gaps, not only the neat stories.
A big wave of your arm can send a simple message across a playground, because the other person sees the movement and knows you mean 'come here' or 'hello'.
Two people can send information with a flashlight by agreeing that one blink means yes and two blinks mean no, even when they are too far to talk.
A whistle can carry a message farther than a speaking voice, so a teacher may use one long blast to mean 'line up' on a noisy field.
Movement, sound, and light only send information if both people agreed on the code first; a random blink does not yet mean a word.
Knocking a pattern on a wall is a sound message that can pass through when you cannot see the other person in the next room.
Raising or lowering a colored flag is a movement-and-color signal people have used so a far partner can see a yes or a no.
A drum can send a planned pattern of beats, a sound code two groups can use when they are too far apart for ordinary talking.
Covering and uncovering a lamp makes long and short flashes of light, a way two people can spell a short message in the dark.
A clap-clap pause clap can mean 'I am ready' if your partner learned that pattern, a sound signal that needs no words.
Pointing your arm at a door sends information with movement: the other person can follow the line of your arm without a spoken sentence.

topic: mirror flash on a sunny day
en: A small mirror can flash sunlight toward a partner on a hill, a light signal that works only if both of you watch for the sparkle.
In a guided activity, talk into a tight-string cup phone and let your partner listen, so you feel how sound can carry a message along the string.
A flat palm held toward someone is a movement that often means stop, a message many people can read even in a noisy street.
A school bell is a sound that sends the same information to many people at once: it is time to gather or time to change activity.
Turning a room light on or off can mean 'I am home' to a family member watching from the yard, a simple light message after dark.

topic: need a clear line for light
en: Light messages need a clear path; a wall blocks the flashlight, so partners must stand where each can see the lamp.
A sound message can fail in a very noisy market, so people may switch to a wave or a light when talking cannot be heard.

topic: need to be seen for movement
en: A movement message only works if the other person is looking; that is why a referee also uses a whistle, a sound, not only an arm signal.
A class can try sending the same word three ways: a gesture, a clap code, and a flashlight code, then talk about which way arrived fastest.
Write the agreed code on paper before you start, so both people remember that two flashes mean 'okay' and three mean 'wait'.
A tiny finger wiggle is hard to see far away, so a bigger movement, a louder sound, or a brighter light carries the message farther.
Information between two people works better if they take turns: one sends the flash or clap, then watches or listens for the reply.
A nod or a head shake is a small movement that can mean yes or no when sound would disturb a quiet room.
A bike horn sends a short sound that means 'I am here', information that helps two people avoid bumping when they cannot yet see each other well.
Holding up a red card or a green card is a movement-and-color message, a cousin of a traffic light that two people can copy in a classroom game.
After each activity, describe how the message traveled: as a movement you saw, a sound you heard, or a light you watched.

topic: choose the channel for the place
en: Pick movement in a quiet library, sound on a foggy field, or light at night, so the way you send information fits the place you are in.
Earth materials are the non-living things that make up the environment, such as rocks, soil, water, and air around a schoolyard.
A rock is an earth material because it is a non-living solid from the ground, even when plants later grow beside it.
Soil is an earth material made of tiny bits of rock, bits of dead plants, air, and water, covering much of the land we walk on.
Water in a river, a puddle, or rain is an earth material: it is non-living, yet it shapes the land and is part of the environment.
The air around you is an earth material too: it is a non-living mixture of gases that fills the space of the environment.
Sand is an earth material made of small, hard grains, often bits of rock or shell, that you can pour but not living on their own.
Clay is a sticky earth material made of very tiny mineral bits; it is non-living even though people shape it into pots.
A living tree is not called an earth material; the soil it stands in and the water it drinks are earth materials around it.
A kalabaw is a living animal, so it is not an earth material, even though it walks on soil and drinks water that are earth materials.
Pebbles in a creek are earth materials: small stones rolled by moving water, non-living pieces of the environment you can pick up.
Mud is soil mixed with extra water, so it is still made of earth materials even when it feels messy under your slippers.
Ice on a mountain or in a freezer is still the earth material water, only in solid form, not a living thing.
Minerals are non-living solids that make up rocks, so both minerals and rocks are earth materials in the environment.
You can walk a schoolyard and name earth materials: the packed soil, the gravel path, the puddle, and the air you breathe.
A plastic wrapper is made by people from processed materials; it is not a natural earth material the way a stone or a clay lump is.
Gravel on a barangay road is an earth material: broken rock pieces used because they are hard, non-living, and easy to spread.

topic: seashells can be mixed in sand
en: Bits of old shells in beach sand are non-living now, so they sit with sand as part of the earth materials of that shore.
Clouds are tiny water drops or ice in the air, so they are earth materials in the sky, not living animals.
The environment means the surroundings of living things, and the non-living parts of those surroundings are what we call earth materials.
A useful class sort is two baskets: living things such as leaves, and earth materials such as stones, dry sand, and a cup of water.
A freshly fallen leaf was part of a living plant, but as it breaks into soil it becomes mixed with earth materials of the ground.
Sea salt left after water dries is a mineral earth material, a non-living solid that was dissolved in ocean water.
Big boulders on a hillside are earth materials too: they are just very large rocks, still non-living pieces of the land.
Earth materials do not eat, grow, or have babies the way living things do, which is a simple test for a stone versus a seedling.
Both the flowing water and the stones in a riverbed are earth materials; the fish living in that river are not.
Dust on a windowsill is often tiny bits of soil or rock, earth materials so small that air can lift them for a while.
Rocks, soil, water, and air can look different, but they share the group name earth materials because they are the non-living environment.
Wet sand at low tide is still an earth material; adding water does not turn the sand into a living thing.
Air is an earth material you cannot hold in your hand the way you hold a pebble, but it still fills the environment around every living thing.
People build with earth materials when they use stone, clay bricks, sand in concrete, or water mixed into mortar, all non-living stuff from the land.
A garden has living plants and also earth materials: the soil, the watering water, the stones at the edge, and the air between the leaves.
Volcanic ash is an earth material: tiny bits of rock from a volcano, non-living even when it covers plants after an eruption.
Rice on a plate is food from a living plant, not an earth material; the soil the rice grew in is the earth material.
Some metals start as minerals in rocks, so the ore in the ground is an earth material before people melt it into a pan or wire.
Rain is the earth material water falling from clouds, a non-living part of the environment that can fill a drum or a river.
A Grade 3 test is to touch and name: this stone is an earth material, this worm is living, this puddle is an earth material.
Old coral rock in a wall is a non-living earth material now, even if living coral animals once built the reef it came from.
Earth materials can move without being alive: wind blows sand, rivers carry pebbles, and gravity pulls rocks down a slope.
We say earth materials the way we say art materials: they are the stuff the environment is made of, only this stuff is non-living nature.
A dry creek bed is still made of earth materials: sand, stones, and packed soil, even when the water has gone for a season.
Steam from a kettle is the earth material water as a gas; it is non-living, like the liquid water it came from.
Earth materials are natural non-living parts of the land, water, and air; a candy wrapper on the path is litter, not an earth material.
In one sentence: earth materials are the non-living rocks, soil, water, and air that make up the environment living things share.

topic: use the name in a walk
en: On a nature walk, practice the name: 'This gravel is an earth material,' so the group word becomes as easy as rock, soil, or water.
PHIVOLCS volcano alert levels are a numbered scale that tells communities how serious the unrest is and what they should prepare to do.
Alert Level 0 means the volcano is quiet, with no extra unrest, so daily life can go on while PHIVOLCS still keeps watching.
Alert Level 1 means low unrest, such as extra steam or small quakes, a time to review family plans even if there is no eruption yet.
Alert Level 2 means unrest is increasing, so communities near the slopes should stay informed and be ready to leave if the next level is raised.
Alert Level 3 means magma is close enough that a hazardous eruption is possible in the coming weeks, so people in danger zones should prepare to evacuate.
Alert Level 4 means a hazardous eruption is possible within days, so people in mapped danger zones should leave before the blast, not after it starts.
Alert Level 5 means a hazardous eruption is underway, so the job is to stay out of the danger zone and follow official rescue and shelter instructions.
Before any eruption, families should know whether their house sits inside a permanent danger zone or a lahar path on a PHIVOLCS map.
Before alerts rise, pack water, food, medicine, and a mask in a go-bag, because leaving is faster when the bag is already by the door.
Before and during unrest, get the alert level from PHIVOLCS or local officials, not from a rumor that the volcano 'looks angry' today.
During a high alert, leave when officials say to leave; staying to watch lava from a close slope is not interpreting the alert, it is ignoring it.
During an eruption, stay out of river valleys that can carry hot flows or lahars, even if the sky above your own roof still looks pale.
During ashfall, stay indoors when you can, close windows, and wear a mask if you must go out, following the alert and ash warnings together.
After the loudest blast, do not rush home until PHIVOLCS lowers the alert and local officials say the roads and slopes are safe enough.
After an eruption, heavy rain can still send lahars down rivers, so a falling alert level does not cancel watching the weather on ash-covered slopes.
After ashfall, wet ash on a roof is heavy, so clear it carefully from a safe stance and never let children play on a loaded roof.

topic: levels can go up or down
en: Alert levels can rise or fall as the instruments change, so a family plan should work both for going away and for a later return.
To interpret an alert level is to turn the number into an action: stay, pack, leave, or stay away, matching what PHIVOLCS and the barangay ask.
On the PHIVOLCS scale, a higher alert number means greater volcanic danger and a stronger call to prepare or to leave mapped zones.

topic: do not wait to see lava
en: Alert Level 4 is already a call to leave danger zones; waiting until you see lava from your window is later than the alert was designed for.
Schools near an active volcano may suspend class as alerts rise, a before-eruption action that follows the same PHIVOLCS numbers families see.
Before a high alert becomes an eruption, farmers in mapped zones are often asked to move animals, because ash and flows can arrive faster than a herd.
During Alert Level 5, do not walk closer for photos; interpreting the alert means treating the eruption as a hazard, not as a show.
Each PHIVOLCS bulletin names the volcano and the alert level, so a Taal alert is not a Mayon alert; read the name before you act.
Before unrest grows, pick a family meeting place outside the danger zone, so during an evacuation no one waits on a close slope for the others.

topic: during: masks and goggles if ash
en: If ash is falling during the eruption, a mask and eye protection help you breathe and see while you stay away from the mapped hot zones.
After ashfall, officials may test drinking water and warn about ash on grass, so returning home includes checking food and water, not only the roof.
A volcano can look calm at Alert Level 3 if magma is still rising inside; the instruments, not the pretty cone, set the number you should follow.
Barangay radios and halls repeat the PHIVOLCS alert so people without internet still hear whether to stay, pack, or leave.
Even at a low alert, the permanent danger zone around an active crater stays off-limits, because sudden explosions have happened there before.
Before an eruption, walk or list the evacuation route to higher ground away from rivers, so during a night alert you are not choosing a path in panic.
During a fast-changing eruption, follow one official stream of PHIVOLCS and local government notices so mixed chat messages do not send you toward a valley.
After people go home, recovering farms and cleaning ash can take a long time, so 'after' is a stage, not a single afternoon.
Alert Level 2 is already a watch, not a time for picnics on the slope; interpreting it means extra caution even before evacuation is ordered.
Before you evacuate, keep copies of IDs and a small radio with the go-bag, so during and after the eruption your family can still be identified and informed.
Around Taal, alerts also mean staying off the lake when officials close it, because an eruption can send hazards across the water as well as the land.

topic: do not return for pets late
en: Take pets when you first leave at a high alert; going back into a danger zone during Alert Level 5 to fetch an animal is not a safe interpretation.
After ashfall, people with breathing trouble should keep using protection and follow health advice, because fine ash can bother lungs even when the sky looks clearer.
A class chart can list each alert number beside a before, during, or after action, so interpreting the scale is a matching job, not a guess.
Low alerts mean unrest that may quiet again; interpreting them still means extra watching, not a claim that an eruption is guaranteed this week.
During heavy ash or explosions, stay in the assigned shelter instead of walking home across open ground, even if the first boom has already passed.
After a big ash-producing eruption, some valleys use rain and river warnings because lahars can come at night days later, long after the crater grows quieter.
Communities near Mayon or Taal practice eruption drills before a crisis, so during a real alert people already know the meeting place and the route.
Interpret the printed hazard map with the alert, not only a memory of the last eruption, because a new blast can still follow old valleys.
Read the PHIVOLCS alert number, match it to before-during-after actions, and do those actions in the mapped zones, not later when the sky is already dark with ash.
Green plants use sunlight to make food in photosynthesis, so almost every lunch on Earth traces back to energy from the Sun.
The Sun warms land and water, and that uneven heating helps make wind, so weather itself depends on sunlight reaching Earth.
Sunlight evaporates water from seas and puddles, starting the water cycle that later brings rain to farms and forests.
Daytime is when our side of Earth faces the Sun, so the Sun times when people can work outdoors without lamps.
After a class discussion, confirm a Sun idea in a trustworthy book or science site, so a guess about sunshine is checked, not just voted on.
Tiny ocean plants use sunlight near the sea surface, so fish that eat them, and people who eat fish, still depend on the Sun.
Without the Sun's heat, Earth would be far too cold for liquid oceans and for the living things that need liquid water.
Most of what we see outdoors in the day is sunlight bouncing off things, so vision in the yard still depends on the Sun.
A solar panel turning sunlight into electricity is a modern check that the Sun's energy is real and useful, not only a story.
The Sun's light hits some parts of Earth more directly in some months, which is why seasons change and crops have planting times.
Write the class suggestions about the Sun first, then tick which ones a textbook or PAGASA education page also states.
Clothes on a line dry faster in sunlight because the Sun's heat helps water evaporate, an everyday importance you can observe at home.
Coal and oil store energy that plants captured from sunlight long ago, so even some fuels in engines began as solar energy.
The Sun matters as a light source and as an energy source, so a complete discussion is more than 'it makes us warm'.
A trustworthy secondary source names an author, a publisher, or an agency, unlike a rumor that 'the Sun will not rise tomorrow'.
Animals cannot eat sunlight, but they eat plants or eat animals that ate plants, so their food energy still started in the Sun.
People still set daily schedules around sunrise and sunset, a social importance of the Sun you can confirm on a clock and a window.
A plant left in a dark cupboard yellows because it is missing sunlight, a classroom check that light is needed, not optional decoration.
Weather reports mention sunshine or cloud because clouds block some sunlight, changing how warm a day feels for people and crops.
If the class votes that the Moon heats the day, a secondary science source can correct it: daytime heat comes from the Sun.
Trees race upward because sunlight is the energy they compete for, so a forest's shape is another sign of the Sun's importance.
Many reef builders live with tiny algae that need sunlit water, so some underwater life still depends on sunlight reaching the shallows.
A finished class list might say: the Sun gives light, heat, food energy for plants, and the timing of day, each ticked against a source.
Wind is moving air, and much of that motion starts because the Sun heats some places more than others, an idea a weather book can confirm.

topic: night reminds us we need the sun
en: At night we use lamps because sunlight is gone, a daily reminder that outdoor seeing and warming were coming from the Sun.
If a classmate invents a temperature for the Sun's surface, leave it off the confirmed list until a trustworthy source states a rounded value.

topic: people need plants that need sun
en: People need oxygen and food that green plants make using sunlight, so the Sun's importance to living things includes us.
Outdoor shadows point away from the Sun, a simple observation that the bright heat and light in the yard come from that one star.
Ice left in sunlight melts faster than ice in shade, a home test that the Sun delivers heat living things and people then use.
A PAGASA or NASA education page is a trustworthy secondary source you can use to confirm class ideas about sunlight and weather.

topic: sun is a star not a planet
en: The Sun is a star, the nearest one, which is why it can light and heat a whole planet; a science book will state that clearly.

topic: clouds and umbrellas still about the sun
en: People use umbrellas and shade because sunlight can be strong, which is another way daily life shows the Sun matters to living things.
Close the discussion by reading two confirmed sentences from a textbook aloud, so the class record is checked science, not only opinions.

topic: predict same time if air small
en: If air resistance is small, you can predict that a heavy stone and a light stone dropped together will hit the ground at about the same time.
A light crumpled paper can fall faster than a flat heavy poster if the poster catches more air, so shape matters as well as weight.
A falling object feels gravity pulling down and air pushing up, so a fair prediction asks which of those two forces matters more this time.
A heavier object feels a stronger pull of gravity, but it is also harder to speed up, so those two effects can cancel in free fall.
Many people predict the heavier object must win, but careful drops show that idea fails when both objects cut through air easily.
Drop two compact stones of different mass from the same height; if they land together, your result matches the gravity prediction, not the heavier-wins guess.
A feather is a poor test of gravity alone because its wide, light shape lets air hold it up, so it does not prove gravity is weaker on feathers.
In a vacuum there is no air to push back, so the remaining force is gravity, and objects with different mass can fall together.
To test the prediction fairly, release both objects from rest at the same height, or a head start will look like a heavier-wins result.
Gravity makes a falling object go faster the longer it falls, and that speeding up is about the same for compact heavy and light objects.
A light, wide object can reach a steady falling speed when air push equals weight, so it stops speeding up while a rock still does.
A parachute is made wide so air resistance becomes large on purpose; that is why a person with a parachute falls more slowly than a dropped bag of rice.
Weight is the pull of gravity on an object; a bigger mass has bigger weight, but that does not by itself make it land first in free fall.
A complete explanation says whether you expect air to matter, and because of that whether the heavier object should land first or not.
A tiny raindrop can fall more slowly than a compact hailstone because air matters more for the drop's small weight and open shape.

topic: do not drop from unsafe height
en: Test the idea from a safe classroom height onto a clear floor; a dangerous drop does not make the gravity explanation more true.
Crumple one sheet of paper into a ball and drop it beside a flat sheet: the ball falls faster, showing air, not missing gravity, slowed the flat sheet.
Use two clay balls, one bigger, so the material is the same; if they land together, mass was not the reason one would have to win.
Write your prediction before you drop anything, then compare the landing with that sentence, or the test cannot change anyone's mind.
Gravity acts on every mass near Earth, light or heavy, which is why both a pebble and a mango are pulled downward when you let go.
Air resistance grows as an object moves faster, so a light wide thing may slow its speeding up while a compact rock keeps gaining speed longer.
On the Moon there is almost no air, so the hammer-and-feather thought is that they land together, a clean gravity prediction without air in the way.

topic: heavier not a stronger downward race
en: Thinking of falling as a race the heavy object must win mixes up weight with acceleration; gravity can speed different masses up the same way.
If you cannot see clearly, listen: two compact objects dropped together often make one shared sound, evidence they arrived together.
If you change shape and mass at once, you cannot tell which change caused a slower fall, so a gravity test should keep shape similar.

topic: gravity still on a floating balloon
en: A helium balloon rising does not mean gravity turned off; a larger upward force from the air is winning for a while, which is a different comparison.
A loose paper falls slowly and a binder falls quickly because air holds the paper, not because gravity forgot the paper's small mass.
Near Earth's surface the gravitational speeding up is about the same for objects in the same classroom, which is why compact drops can match.
Say 'I predict they land together because air will not matter much' or the opposite, so the explanation is inside the prediction, not added later.
A heavy backpack and a light water bottle, both compact, can fall together from a safe height, challenging the idea that heavier always wins.

topic: air is a force not a maybe
en: Air resistance is a real force you can feel on a fast bike; it is the extra reason some light objects lose the falling 'race'.
Never test falling by dropping animals or people; the competency is about objects, and a safe classroom drop is enough to see the pattern.
If one object is compact and one is fluffy, they may not land together, and the honest explanation is air, not a failure of gravity.
Heavier objects do not automatically fall faster; they do so only when air resistance treats them differently, not because gravity prefers heavy things.
A PAGASA Public Storm Warning Signal is a number that matches how strong the winds are expected to be in a named place.
Signal Number 1 means strong winds of about 39 to 61 kilometers per hour are expected, enough to snap twigs and make sea travel rough for small boats.
Under Signal 1, expect cloudy to rainy weather and a steadily strengthening wind, not yet the most destructive typhoon winds.
Signal Number 2 means gale-force winds of about 62 to 88 kilometers per hour, which can break small branches and bother light houses.
When Signal 2 is up, sea travel is more dangerous and some classes or work may stop, matching winds too strong for ordinary outdoor days.
Signal Number 3 means stormy winds of about 89 to 117 kilometers per hour, with heavy rain likely and a real risk of damage to many roofs.
Under Signal 3, people are expected to stay indoors away from windows, because flying debris and hard rain make outdoor weather unsafe.
